title: Solving General QUBOs with Warm-Start QAOA via a Reduction to Max-Cut
journal_or_venue: ACM Transactions on Quantum Computing (preprint / arXiv:2504.06253v2)
abstract_summary: The paper introduces a method to solve general QUBO instances with warm-start QAOA by reducing QUBOs to equivalent Max-Cut problems (adding one auxiliary variable) and leveraging semidefinite-program (SDP) based warm-starts (Goemans–Williamson and Burer–Monteiro relaxations) to construct biased initial states. The authors empirically compare this Max-Cut–based SDP warm-start against a direct QUBO relaxation warm-start on a variety of small (≤16-variable) problem classes (random QUBOs, TSP, portfolio optimization, MIS) and find that the best warm-start choice is strongly problem-dependent, with the 2D GW projection plus a rotation on the auxiliary vertex often performing best at low circuit depth.
methodology_description: The authors study warm-start strategies for QAOA applied to general QUBOs by (1) mapping arbitrary QUBOs to equivalent Max-Cut instances via a standard reduction that introduces one auxiliary qubit/variable; (2) producing warm-start separable initial states from semidefinite relaxations of Max-Cut (Goemans–Williamson projection to k=2 or k=3, and Burer–Monteiro BM2/BM3) or from a direct continuous relaxation of the QUBO (QUBO-Relaxed); (3) optionally applying a “vertex-at-top” global rotation to individual qubits (first, last, or none) before encoding onto Bloch-sphere single-qubit states; and (4) running QAOA with those warm-start initial states and optimizing circuit parameters classically. They benchmark these warm-start methods (GW2/GW3, BM2/BM3, and QUBO-Relaxed with different numbers of random initializations) across 1000 instances of several problem classes (random QUBOs, Travelling Salesman, Portfolio Optimization, Maximum Independent Set) in 16-variable QUBOs (mapped to 17-vertex Max-Cut graphs), evaluate performance at depth p=0 for all instances and p=1..5 for a subset of 10 instances per problem, and report aggregated metrics (normalized approximation ratio and optimal-sampling probability) with means and standard deviations.
algorithms_used: Goemans–Williamson SDP relaxation (projected to k=2 or k=3)
Geometric Brownian Motion (for portfolio price simulation)
experimental_setup: All experiments were simulated classically using a custom QAOA simulator based on Lykov et al. (Fast simulation of high-depth QAOA circuits). No quantum hardware was used. Warm-start vector computations used SDP/BM solvers and local optimization routines run on classical hardware.
dataset_used: For portfolio optimization, synthetic financial time series were generated by Geometric Brownian Motion: n=16 assets, N=250 time steps, S0=1, drifts µ_i sampled uniformly from [-0.05,0.05], volatilities σ_i sampled uniformly from [-0.20,0.20]. From simulated returns the mean vector µ and covariance Σ were computed and used to build a 16-variable QUBO. Other datasets were synthetic combinatorial instances: random QUBOs (continuous uniform in [-1,1] or discrete ±1), TSP (5 cities with coordinates uniform on [-1,1]^2 mapped to a 16-variable QUBO after symmetry elimination), MIS on random graphs (Erdős–Rényi GNP and Newman–Watts–Strogatz ensembles, n=16).

experiment_input.preprocessing: For portfolio: compute returns r_{i,k}, mean µ and covariance Σ, then build QUBO per Eq. (38). For TSP/MIS: construct quadratic cost matrices with penalty terms and map to QUBO. All QUBOs then optionally reduced to Max-Cut adjacency using the specified mapping that introduces an auxiliary vertex.

overview_steps: Generate 1000 instances per problem type (random QUBOs, TSP, Portfolio, MIS).
For each QUBO instance, form the corresponding Max-Cut adjacency matrix A by adding one auxiliary vertex (17th) as per Eq. (7)/(8).
Compute semidefinite relaxations on the Max-Cut formulation: GW relaxation (full-dimension), and low-dimension Burer–Monteiro (BM2/BM3).
For GW→k projection: sample random orthonormal bases, project GW vectors into k=2 or k=3 subspace, keep the projection maximizing trace(J^T Y^T Y); 50 random bases sampled.
For BM2/BM3: optimize factor vectors via randomized stochastic perturbations (step size η=0.05, 100 iterations).
Compute QUBO-Relaxed warmstart by maximizing y^T Q y over y in [0,1]^n using L-BFGS-B with epsilon=0.1. Run with multiple random initializations (10 and 50) to compare sensitivity.

Map relaxation outputs (vectors or continuous y) to single-qubit Bloch-sphere angles to form separable warm-start state |ψ_init〉 (k=2/3 encodings). Optionally apply vertex-at-top rotation on first, last, or none qubit.

Run QAOA with cost Hamiltonian chosen either as HQ_Q (direct QUBO) or HM_A (Max-Cut adjacency) using the warm-start initial state and a separable mixing Hamiltonian equal to the maximum-eigenvalue product state. Depths p=0..5; p=0 for all 1000 instances, and p=1..5 for 10 selected instances per problem.

Optimize QAOA parameters using COBYLA with 10 classical restarts per circuit: if p=1 all 10 initializations uniform; if p>1 use 9 uniform and one taken as best from p-1. Select best of 10 optimized parameter sets.

Evaluate metrics (normalized approximation ratio α and optimal-sampling probability P) per instance, aggregate mean and standard deviation across instances, and compare warm-start variants and vertex-at-top choices.

P: optimal-sampling probability = sum_{optimal basis states} |〈φ|ψ〉|^2

Comparisons between warm-start methods (GW2, GW3, BM2, BM3, QUBO-Relaxed with 10/50 initializations)
Ablation over vertex-at-top rotations (first, last, none)

experiment_output.formats: Aggregated numeric tables and plots of α and P vs QAOA depth p; probability density plots of α over random basis states.

Experiments are classical simulations; exact reproduction requires the custom simulator implementation and the provided code repository. key_findings: [supported] Any QUBO can be mapped to a Max-Cut instance by introducing a single auxiliary variable/qubit; the paper provides the explicit mapping and a derivation (Eq. 7–8, Appendix A).

[supported] Applying semidefinite-program (SDP) based warm-starts (Goemans–Williamson projections, BM2/BM3) to the Max-Cut instance obtained from the QUBO mapping is a viable way to warm-start QAOA for general QUBOs (empirically evaluated up to 16 variables).

[supported] The best warm-start method is problem-dependent: different QUBO problem classes (random QUBOs, TSP, portfolio optimization, MIS) favor different warm-start choices and metrics (approximation ratio vs optimal-sampling probability).

[supported] Goemans–Williamson projected to 2 dimensions (GW2) with a vertex-at-top rotation on the auxiliary (last) qubit often produced the strongest overall performance among SDP-based warm-starts in these experiments.

[supported] The auxiliary qubit introduced by the QUBO→Max-Cut reduction is frequently the best vertex to rotate to the Bloch 'top' in the vertex-at-top heuristic, reducing the need to try O(n) different rotations.

[supported] Burer–Monteiro low-dimension relaxations (BM2/BM3) can give comparable instance-specific approximation ratios but tend to produce significantly lower optimal-sampling probabilities (i.e., produce superpositions with less weight on exact optima) in these experiments.

[supported] The QUBO-relaxation warm-start (continuous relaxation of x in [0,1]^n) is highly sensitive to the nonconvex optimizer's initialization; increasing the number of random initializations (e.g., 10 → 50) improved performance on several problem classes.

[supported] For portfolio optimization (where the QUBO relaxation is convex/tractable), GW2 warm-starts still produced higher instance-specific approximation ratios and substantially higher optimal-sampling probabilities than the direct QUBO-relaxation warm-start in the conducted experiments.
[supported] Warm-started QAOA (SDP-based warm-starts) yields better approximation metrics at shallow depths (p up to 5) in the studied instances, consistent with prior warm-start literature.

[speculative] Because the auxiliary qubit often is best for the vertex-at-top rotation, this observation could be used generally to reduce warm-start overhead from O(n) rotation trials (the claim is motivated by experiments here but presented as a broader heuristic).

[speculative] The paper suggests that differences in warm-start performance across problem types stem from structural features (e.g., constraint terms producing skewed alpha distributions), but a full theoretical explanation is left for future work.

[disputed] The paper does not claim nor provide evidence of a practical quantum advantage over classical algorithms for these QUBOs; any implication that these warm-starts yield a device-level or asymptotic quantum advantage would contradict the presented scope (small-scale simulations) and is not made by the authors.
results_summary: The authors introduce and evaluate a pipeline that reduces arbitrary QUBO instances to Max-Cut by adding one auxiliary variable, then applies SDP-based warm-start strategies (Goemans–Williamson projections and low-rank Burer–Monteiro relaxations) to initialize QAOA. Empirical simulations on 16-variable problems across random QUBOs, travelling-salesman, portfolio optimization, and maximum independent set show that GW2 (Goemans–Williamson projected to 2D) with a rotation on the auxiliary (last) qubit frequently yields the best instance-specific approximation ratios and, in some cases (notably portfolio optimization), much higher probabilities of sampling the exact optimum. BM2/BM3 can match approximation ratios but often produce poorer optimal-sampling probabilities. The direct QUBO-continuous relaxation warm-start's performance depends strongly on the number of random initializations used in the (nonconvex) solver. Overall, the optimal warm-start choice is strongly problem- and metric-dependent.
performance_claims: GW2 (with last-vertex-at-top rotation) achieved instance-specific approximation ratios around 0.93 ± 0.21 on discrete random QUBOs (p up to 5) while yielding an optimal-sampling probability ≈ 0.22 ± 0.22 (Figure 6). [supported]

For portfolio-optimization instances (n = 16, budget B = 8), GW2 produced extremely high instance-specific approximation ratios (e.g., ≈ 0.9987 ± 0.0052 for a rotation choice) and high optimal-sampling probabilities (≈ 0.91 ± 0.24), outperforming the direct QUBO-relaxation warm-start on both metrics. [supported]

BM2/BM3 relaxations achieved comparable instance-specific approximation ratios (e.g., BM2 ≈ 0.9661 ± 0.0063 for portfolio) but had near-zero optimal-sampling probabilities (e.g., BM2 P ≈ 0.0009 ± 0.0057 for portfolio), indicating produced states are superpositions of high-cost but non-optimal bitstrings. [supported]

QUBO-relaxation warm-start performance improves with more random initializations in the nonconvex solver; experiments compared 10 vs 50 initializations and found noticeable gains for constrained problems (TSP, MIS). [supported]

Vertex-at-top rotation on the auxiliary (last) qubit consistently ranked better than rotating a random non-auxiliary qubit or performing no rotation across most tested problem classes (except TSP where 'no rotation' performed better for P in one metric). [supported]
quantum_advantage_detail: The paper reports small-scale (≤17 vertex) simulated QAOA experiments comparing warm-start initialization strategies; it does not claim or demonstrate a quantum computational advantage over classical algorithms or provable asymptotic speedups. Results are improvements in variational initialization and sampling behavior on benchmark instances, not demonstrations of device-level or asymptotic quantum advantage.
limitations: Experiments limited to small instances (QUBOs up to 16 variables / corresponding Max-Cut with 17 vertices).
QUBO-Relaxed warmstart requires solving a non-convex / NP-Hard relaxation for general Q, so performance depends strongly on local optimization and number of random initializations (no guarantees).

BM2/BM3 relaxations produce comparatively low optimal sampling probabilities even when instance-specific approximation ratios are competitive (i.e., warmstarts can bias towards high-cost suboptimal superpositions).
Depth of QAOA analyzed is low (p ≤ 5); conclusions drawn at low depth may not hold at larger depths.
Performance comparisons and conclusions are metric-dependent (approximation ratio vs probability of sampling optimal solution), so no single warmstart universally dominates.
The mapping from QUBO to Max-Cut introduces an auxiliary qubit/variable and degeneracy (e.g., y and −y map to same x), which changes problem structure and may affect results.

The QUBO→Max-Cut mapping and the vertex-at-top heuristic require testing rotations; while the auxiliary qubit is often best, the procedure can impose overhead (authors note an O(n) overhead in general).

QAOA parameter optimization uses classical local optimizers (COBYLA, L-BFGS-B) with limited restarts (10 runs for QAOA, 10 or 50 initializations for QUBO-Relaxed), so results are sensitive to classical optimizer choices and may get stuck in local optima.
Experiments were performed with a classical QAOA simulator (no noisy hardware experiments reported), so hardware noise and device constraints were not assessed. [inferred]
[inferred] Limited exploration of other QAOA design choices (different mixers, encodings, or parameter heuristics) beyond the warm-start/state-preparation strategies considered.

[inferred] The empirical results may not generalize to much larger problem sizes or different instance distributions due to testing on specific ensembles (random, TSP with 5 cities, specific graph models, portfolio settings).
open_questions: What are the mechanisms that cause different warm-start approaches (GW2 via QUBO→Max-Cut vs QUBO-Relaxed) to perform better or worse depending on problem type and metric?
How do the observed trends scale with problem size (n » 16) and deeper QAOA circuits (larger p)?
Can the dependence of QUBO-Relaxed performance on the number of random initializations be reduced (better solvers, global methods, or problem-specific heuristics)?
How robust are the warm-start strategies to realistic hardware noise, gate errors, and connectivity constraints?
Does the addition of the auxiliary qubit in the QUBO→Max-Cut mapping create structural artifacts (symmetries or degeneracies) that limit performance for certain problem classes?
How should one choose between warm-start strategies for a new problem instance given only limited prior information (i.e., can reliable selection rules be developed)?
What is the trade-off between optimizing approximation ratio (expected cost) versus maximizing the sampling probability of the optimal solution when using warm-starts?
Are there theoretical performance guarantees or bounds for warm-started QAOA when applying the QUBO→Max-Cut reduction (analogous to GW approximation bounds)?
How effective are vertex-at-top heuristics in general, and can the search/overhead for selecting the best vertex be reduced beyond the auxiliary-qubit observation?
How do alternative SDP/Burer–Monteiro parameterizations or random-projection strategies (different k or projection sampling schemes) affect warm-start quality?
future_work: Better understanding the mechanisms behind the observed differences in warm-start performance across problem types and metrics (explicitly mentioned by the authors).

Scaling experiments to larger problem sizes and investigating the need for more iterations / random initializations for QUBO-Relaxed on larger instances (authors note expectation that larger problems will require more iterations).
Studying and formalizing heuristics for vertex-at-top selection (including exploiting the auxiliary qubit in the QUBO→Max-Cut mapping to reduce overhead).
Improving or replacing the non-convex optimization used for QUBO-Relaxed warmstarts to reduce sensitivity to initializations and provide more reliable solutions.
Evaluating warm-started QAOA variants on noisy quantum hardware and assessing the interplay between warm-start benefits and device noise/error rates.

key_ideas: #idea:hybrid-approach — Map general QUBOs to Max-Cut (introducing one auxiliary vertex) and compute SDP/Burer–Monteiro relaxations classically to produce separable warm-start states for QAOA.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Demonstrates practical warm-start strategies that improve low-depth (p=0..5) QAOA performance on small (≤16-variable) instances, emphasizing NISQ-era relevance.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Compares GW2/GW3 projections, BM2/BM3 factorizations, and direct QUBO continuous relaxations as classical preprocessing steps feeding into QAOA parameter optimization.
#idea:near-term-feasibility — Empirical benchmarking across 1000 instances per problem class (random QUBOs, TSP, MIS, portfolio optimization) shows warm-start choice is strongly problem-dependent.
#idea:hybrid-approach — A 2D Goemans–Williamson projection combined with a rotation on the auxiliary (mapped) vertex often achieves the best performance at low circuit depth.
#idea:hybrid-approach — Uses separable Bloch-sphere encodings of relaxation vectors to keep warm-start states shallow and amenable to classical parameter optimization (COBYLA).
